newsitem.title: USA: PepsiCo seen thriving without restaurants.
newsitem.headline: PepsiCo seen thriving without restaurants.

text.p: Colonel Sanders and the Pepsi Generation are expected to part ways as PepsiCo Inc spins off its vast chain-restaurant operation, a break that analysts say would make PepsiCo a Wall Street favorite.

The colonel's KFC -- the old Kentucky Fried Chicken -- Pizza Hut and Taco Bell make up almost 30,000 restaurants around the world that have labored in recent years under intense competition, thinning margins and slow growth.

"It makes sense because the restaurants were a real driver of Pepsi until about two years ago. It was a dynamic growth business but the category has become significantly more competitive," said David Adelman, analyst at Dean Witter, who called the resturing "highly likely."

"It does not have the growth prospects of five or ten years ago, so it is better for Pepsi to concentrate on high growth categorires -- soft drinks and Frito," he said, referring to PepsiCo's salty snack food division.
Pepsi declined to comment on the spin-off, a spokesman saying only that the board of directors is meeting Thursday.
But Wall Street cheered the possibility of a break, first reported in the Wall Street Journal.
PepsiCo shares surged 2-3/4 to 34-1/2 in extremely heavy New York Stock Exchange trade, easing off an earlier high of 35-3/4 this morning.
By midafternoon, 20 million shares had been traded, five times the stock's average daily volume, making its by far the market's most active.
Such broadly-based investor approval of a spin-off would almost force the directors to place the topic on the meeting agenda if in the unlikley event it was not already there, Adelman said.
"A spin-off would likely start a period where the stock will perform very well after stubbing their toe in international soft drinks and the domestic restaurants," he added.
The Purchase, N.Y. company took a 1996 third quarter $376 million after-tax charge related to its international operations, cutting earnings per share to $0.09 versus $0.39 in the year-ago period.
The international debacle was related primarilty to losses at Buenos Aires Embotelladora SA, PepsiCo's largest bottler outside the United States in which it held a one-quarter stake.
The mess and related charge ended a two-year bull run for PepsiCo shares, which climbed to a high of almost 36 last July from about 15 in the summer of 1994.

Thursday afternoon, PepsiCo announced that the board decalred a regular quarterly dividend of $11.5 per share, and company spokespeople were not available to say if the board meeting had concluded, or if additional statements were forthcoming.
Paul Westra, Salomon Bros restaurant analyst, said the fast-food restaurant industry has turned "supercompetitive."
"There is a tit-for-tat strategy among competitors and once you get into a price war, its hard to get out. Just look at all those 99-cent specials."
The restaurant operations in 1995 accounted for 37 percent of the company's $30.42 billion in revenue and 24 percent of profits, which were $1.6 billion, or $1.00 per share.
Beverages accounted for 35 percent of revenue and 37 percent of profits and snack foods were 28 percent of 1995 revenue and 39 percent of profits.
"PepsiCo is looking to exit a business with low return on capital," Westra said.
He said his top restaurant pick is McDonald's Corp, which jumped 1-3/4 to 47 in Thursday afternoon NYSE trade.

"McDonalds is almost entirely focused on the international prospects, which I believe are enormously under-rated by the market. McDonald has a 20-year head start on their (PepsiCo's) brands. While KFC is enormously sucessful in the Pacific Rim, else, their brands elsewhere are only modestly successful."
McDonald's reported 1995 revenue of $9.8 billion and a net profit of $1.43 billion, or $1.97 per share.
((--Intindola, Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1734)).
